```{r packages}
#install.packages() is not called anywhere in this file. 

library(readr)
library(lmtest)
library(tseries)
library(forecast)
library(sandwich)
library(zoo)

library(kableExtra)

```{r load-data}

raw_data <- read_csv("fred_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Base period for real prices: August 2026 dollars
cpi_ref <- raw_data$CPIAUCSL[raw_data$observation_date == as.Date("2026-08-01")]

gas <- raw_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(TRFVOLUSM227NFWA)) %>%                            # Jan 1999 - Aug 2026
  mutate(vmt_pc  = TRFVOLUSM227NFWA * 1e6 / (CNP16OV * 1e3),      # miles/person 16+/month
         rgas    = GASREGCOVM * cpi_ref / CPIAUCSL,               # real $/gal (Aug-2026 $)
         rdpi_pc = DSPIC96 * 1e9 / (CNP16OV * 1e3),               # 2017 $/person/yr
         unrate  = UNRATE,
         umcsent = UMCSENT,
         ln_vmt = log(vmt_pc),
         ln_rgas = log(rgas),
         ln_rdpi = log(rdpi_pc)) %>%
  select(observation_date, vmt_pc, rgas, unrate, rdpi_pc, umcsent, ln_vmt, ln_rgas, ln_rdpi)

# Monthly time series object (Oct 2025 stays NA; it is missing in the source)
gas.ts <- ts(as.matrix(gas[, -1]), start = c(1999, 1), end = c(2026, 8), frequency = 12)
```

# 1. Question and Hypothesis

Does a rise in the real price of gasoline reduce how much Americans drive? We expect that the coefficient on the real gas price will be *negative*, thus signifying an inverse relationship between real gasoline prices and miles driven per person. Higher gas prices raise the cost of driving, incentivizing Americans to drive fewer miles or resort to alternative means of transportation as a cost-saving measure.

# 2. Data

**(a) Source and structure.**\
Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, FRED, \url{https://fred.stlouisfed.org}; series TRFVOLUSM227NFWA (vehicle miles traveled; FHWA), GASREGCOVM (regular gasoline price; EIA), CPIAUCSL (CPI-U, SA; BLS), UNRATE (BLS), DSPIC96 (real disposable personal income; BEA), UMCSENT (University of Michigan), CNP16OV (population 16+; BLS), each at \url{https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/<ID>}.

Accessed: October 20, 2026; version: FRED vintage at download (latest VMT observation Aug 2026). Unit of observation: the United States in one calendar month. Structure: single-unit aggregate time series, $N=1$, $T=332$ months (Jan 1999--Aug 2026); 331 months are usable because CPI, unemployment, income and population are missing in the source for Oct 2025.\

**(b) Variables.**
```{r variable_table}

vartab <- data.frame(
  Variable   = c("ln_vmt", "ln_rgas", "unrate", "ln_rdpi", "umcsent"),
  Definition = c("Log of vehicle miles traveled per person aged 16+",
                 "Log of regular gasoline price deflated by CPI-U",
                 "Civilian unemployment rate",
                 "Log of real disposable income per person aged 16+",
                 "Consumer sentiment"),
  Units      = c("Log of miles per person per month",
                 "Log of Aug-2026 $ per gallon",
                 "Percent",
                 "Log of 2017 $ per person annually",
                 "Index (1966Q1 = 100)"),
  Role       = c("Outcome", "Main regressor", "Control",
                 "Control", "Control")
)
kable(vartab, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE,
      align = c("l", "p{2.6in}", "p{1.4in}", "p{1.1in}"),
      caption = "Variable Definitions") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position")
```

**(c) Data Structure Justification**\
Our hypothesis' focus on the response to changes in real gas prices requires tracking the variation in response/impact over time versus being expressed in single-period units. Further, the monthly nature of a time series data structure allows for immediate and long term effects to changing real gas prices to be studied. However, the structure cannot reveal individual responses from households or regions, only the shifting trends in aggregate responses.

# 3. Identification and Method
The main reason our coefficient might not reflect a causal effect is omitted variables. For example, global economic booms/downturns can shift both oil prices and demand for driving. Meanwhile, increasingly more fuel efficient vehicles can make each mile driven cheaper. Both factors correlate with gas prices but are absent from our model, possibly biasing the coefficient. Furthermore, we expect serial correlation between monthly errors in our time series data in a manner more complex than an AR(1) pattern. Thus, we expect having to use HAC (Newey-West) standard errors alongside differencing if needed.

# 4. Background
**1. Hughes, Knittel, & Sperling (2008).** \url{https://doi.org/10.3386/w12530}\
(i) Setting and data: Monthly U.S. aggregates of per capita gasoline consumption, real gasoline prices, and real disposable income compared across 1975--1980 and 2001--2006. (ii) Method: Log-log OLS with month fixed effects and Newey-West standard errors; 2SLS with oil supply disruptions as a robustness check. (iii) Findings:Short-run price elasticity of gasoline demand was negative: $-0.21$ to $-0.34$ in 1975--1980, but only $-0.034$ to $-0.077$ in 2001--2006. (iv) Relation: We study miles driven, not gasoline sold, through 2026.

**2. Small & Van Dender (2007).** \url{https://doi.org/10.5547/ISSN0195-6574-EJ-Vol28-No1-2}\
(i) Setting and data: Annual panel of U.S. states, 1966--2001, covering vehicle travel, fuel cost per mile, income and fuel efficiency. (ii) Method: Simultaneous-equations model treating fuel efficiency as endogenous. (iii) Findings: Driving elasticity with respect to fuel cost per mile of $-0.045$ short run and $-0.22$ long run, falling to $-0.022$ and $-0.107$ by 1997--2001. (iv) Relation: We use national monthly data, leaving fuel efficiency as an omitted variable.

**3. Gillingham (2014).** \url{https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/regeco/v47y2014icp13-24.html}\
(i) Setting and data: California smog-check odometer records, 2005--2009, for all new vehicles registered in 2001--2003. (ii) Method: Vehicle-level regression analysis of the post-2005 gasoline price surge. (iii) Findings: Medium-run elasticity of miles driven with respect to gasoline price of $-0.22$, varying across households and regions. (iv) Relation: We estimate the aggregate national response using monthly data through 2026, including post-pandemic years.

# 5. Evidence of Data

```{r summary-stats, results='asis'}

vars <- c("ln_vmt", "ln_rgas", "unrate", "ln_rdpi", "umcsent")
gas_complete <- na.omit(gas[vars]) ##removing any incomplete cases to ensure same amount of observations

stats <- data.frame(
  Variable = vars,
  Mean = sapply(gas_complete, mean),
  SD   = sapply(gas_complete, sd),
  Min  = sapply(gas_complete, min),
  Max  = sapply(gas_complete, max),
  Obs  = sapply(gas_complete, length)
)
kable(stats, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE,
      caption = "Summary statistics, monthly, Jan 1999--Aug 2026") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position")
```

```{r ts-figure, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 6.5, fig.align = "center", fig.cap = "Most model variables display non-stationarity through trends while log vehicle miles driven shows seasonality and a drastic 2020 drop, so we expect to difference the data to adjust for seasonality and the pandemic"}

## Stationarity Check, Revealing Trends and/or Seasonality that Call for Future Differencing in our Model
## Time Series Data for ALL Regressed Variables [Even Control]

stationarity_check <- gas.ts[, vars]
colnames(stationarity_check) <- c("ln_vmt (log miles)", "ln_rgas (log $/gal)", "unrate (%)", "ln_rdpi (log$)", "umcsent (index)")

plot.ts(stationarity_check,
        main = "Figure 1: Checking Stationary Within All Model Regressors",
        xlab = "Year",
        mar.multi = c(1, 8, 1, 2)) ##Adding Small Space Between Each Time Series Visualization

```
